common_name: Oratia Beauty Hebe (Variegated Cream-Edged Foliage Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in sharply drained soil; some afternoon shade in hot climates helps keep the cream variegation from scorching.

directions: This slow-growing hebe is grown chiefly for its glossy green leaves edged in a wide band of creamy yellow-white, which hold their color through most of the year. Short spikes of small lavender flowers appear in late spring but are secondary to the foliage display. Watch for any shoots that revert to plain green and prune them out promptly, since reverted growth is more vigorous and will eventually overtake the variegated form. Give it gritty, well-drained soil and avoid winter wet, which causes more hebe losses than cold itself.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil; the foliage color develops most intensely where plants get cool nights and full sun.

directions: A rounded, medium-sized hebe whose dark green leaves flush bronze-purple as temperatures cool, deepening to a rich aubergine shade through autumn and winter before greening up again in spring. Spikes of lavender-blue flowers appear in summer and draw bees steadily through the season. It is one of the more reliably hardy garden hebes and holds up well as informal low hedging or a mixed-border anchor. Trim lightly after flowering to maintain a dense shape, and plant in soil that drains freely since standing winter moisture is its main vulnerability.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

common_name: Wiri Blush Hebe (Pale Pink Long-Flowering Shrub)

planting.note: Plant in spring in gritty, free-draining soil; deadheading spent spikes encourages the next flush of bloom.

directions: Part of the Wiri series of hebes bred in Auckland, New Zealand for compact habit and an extended bloom season, this cultivar carries glossy mid-green leaves and short, dense spikes of pale pink flowers that fade toward white as they age. Flowering runs from spring well into autumn, far longer than most hebe cultivars manage. Shear off spent flower spikes to keep new ones coming, and set plants in sharply drained soil since root rot in wet winter ground is the main threat. Its tidy rounded shape suits low hedging, mixed borders, and large containers.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil; this species flowers earlier than most hebes, often starting in late winter in mild climates.

directions: A New Zealand native species with a dense, twiggy habit and small, narrow, glossy leaves on fine stems. It produces an unusually heavy flush of small white to pale lilac flowers in late winter and early spring, well ahead of most other hebes, making it valuable for early-season color and pollinator forage. It tolerates a bit more shade than many hebe cultivars and benefits from it in hot-summer climates. Prune lightly right after flowering to maintain a full, twiggy shape, and keep it out of heavy or waterlogged soils.

common_name: Carl Teschner Hebe (Dwarf Trailing Groundcover Shrub)

planting.note: Plant in spring in gritty, well-drained soil; this is one of the hardiest and most forgiving groundcover hebes.

directions: One of the most widely planted dwarf hebes, this low spreading selection forms a tight mound of tiny dark green leaves on wiry, purple-tinged stems. In late spring to early summer it is smothered in small violet-blue flowers marked with a white eye, putting on one of the showiest displays of any groundcover hebe. It roots easily from cuttings and tolerates more cold than most larger hebe cultivars, making it a good choice for rockeries, wall tops, and edging in cooler gardens. Shear lightly after flowering to keep growth dense and avoid soil that stays wet through winter.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Plant in spring in sharply drained soil; it tolerates coastal wind and salt spray better than many hebe cultivars.

directions: A naturally occurring New Zealand hybrid grown for its tidy, mounded habit and closely packed grey-green foliage, which gives it a quieter, more textural presence than brighter-leaved hebes. Short spikes of white flowers appear freely in early summer but are secondary to the foliage effect. It handles coastal exposure and salty wind well, making it a dependable choice for seaside gardens. Keep it in gritty, free-draining soil and give it a light trim after flowering to prevent the bare, leggy growth hebes can develop with age.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil; its vigorous upright habit needs more room than most hebe cultivars.

directions: One of the most popular and vigorous of the larger garden hebes, producing long, arching racemes of violet-purple flowers that fade gradually to near white as they age, giving each spike a two-toned effect. It blooms continuously from midsummer well into autumn, outlasting most other hebe cultivars. New growth is flushed red-purple before maturing to glossy mid-green. Use it as an informal flowering hedge or a substantial border shrub, and give it a light trim in spring to remove any winter-damaged tips and keep the shape full.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants after frost danger has passed; in cold climates grow it in a container and overwinter under glass.

directions: A Canary Islands endemic subshrub with large, wrinkled, sage-green leaves whose texture recalls betony or lamb's ears. It produces dense, upright spikes of rose-pink to purplish-red flowers over an unusually long season, often flowering in winter in mild coastal climates where little else is in bloom. It is a fixture of Mediterranean and coastal gardens in zones 9-11 and also makes a striking container or conservatory plant where winters are too cold for it outdoors. Cut stems back hard in spring to control legginess and renew flowering wood, and give it full sun with lean, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container stock in spring in lean, well-drained, alkaline soil.

directions: A low, mounding Mediterranean relative of shrubby germander, with small aromatic grey-green leaves and clusters of pale to bright yellow flowers through summer, an unusual flower color within a genus dominated by blues and purples. It thrives in lean, alkaline, sharply drained soil and tolerates intense heat and drought once established. Use it in rock gardens, dry gravel borders, or Mediterranean-style plantings alongside lavender and rosemary. Shear lightly after the main flowering flush to keep the mound tidy and encourage a second, lighter bloom.

common_name: Ackermann's Germander (Silver-Leaved Prostrate Rock Garden Germander)

planting.note: Plant in spring in extremely sharp-draining soil or scree; winter wet is far more damaging than cold.

directions: A Spanish native dwarf germander that forms a tight, prostrate mat of small, felted, silvery leaves. Bright magenta-pink flowers are held just above the foliage over a long summer season, giving strong color contrast against the silver mat. It is a favorite for troughs, scree beds, dry stone walls, and rock gardens, where sharp drainage is easy to provide. Take cuttings in summer to propagate, since it can be short-lived in gardens with heavy or poorly drained soil, and avoid overhead watering that keeps the foliage wet.
